failing_part: mtry floor(p/3) for a class outcome and floor(√p) for a numeric outcome
narrowest_regime: 500 trees and one with-replacement bootstrap of n rows per tree are the defaults in both packages; the mtry part holds in neither package as written
reason: The mtry rule is backwards. randomForest documents sqrt(p) for classification and p/3 for regression. ranger uses floor(sqrt(p)) for every outcome type, so 'floor(p/3)' is not ranger's default for either outcome. ntree/num.trees = 500, replace = TRUE and sampsize = n (sample.fraction = 1) are right.

citations.cite: randomForest R documentation, ?randomForest (Liaw & Wiener), mtry defaults sqrt(p) classification / p/3 regression
ranger R documentation, ?ranger (Wright & Ziegler 2017, J Stat Softw 77(1)), mtry default floor(sqrt(p))
Liaw A, Wiener M. Classification and Regression by randomForest. R News 2002;2(3):18-22

bite_note: A classifier would get p/3 candidates per split instead of sqrt(p): with large p that means less decorrelated, slower trees, and both accuracy and importance rankings shift. A regression forest would get sqrt(p) instead of p/3. The app would also be calling its default 'the packages' default' when it is not, so results would not reproduce in R.

failing_part: the E-value is RR + √(RR − 1), so a risk ratio of 2 has an E-value of 3
narrowest_regime: none as written; the correct formula is E = RR + √(RR(RR − 1)), which gives 3.41 for RR = 2
reason: The E-value is the common value E at which the Ding-VanderWeele bounding factor E²/(2E − 1) equals RR. Solving E² − 2·RR·E + RR = 0 gives E = RR + √(RR(RR − 1)), so RR = 2 gives 2 + √2 ≈ 3.41. With E = 3 the bounding factor is 9/5 = 1.8 < 2, so a confounder of strength 3 cannot explain the association away. The EValue R package (Mathur, VanderWeele et al.) computes x + sqrt(x*(x − 1)).

citations.cite: VanderWeele TJ, Ding P. Sensitivity analysis in observational research: introducing the E-value. Ann Intern Med 2017;167:268-274
Ding P, VanderWeele TJ. Sensitivity analysis without assumptions. Epidemiology 2016;27:368-377 (bounding factor RR_EU·RR_UD/(RR_EU+RR_UD−1))
EValue R package source, threshold(): x + sqrt(x*(x - true)) / true

bite_note: Every E-value comes out too small, because √(RR − 1) < √(RR(RR − 1)) whenever RR > 1. At RR = 2 the app would report 3 instead of 3.41, so a finding looks more fragile to unmeasured confounding than it is. The CI-limit E-values are wrong in the same direction.

failing_part: q = floor((2*tau - 1)*p) keeps the expected number of falsely selected predictors at or below 1
narrowest_regime: The bound gives E(V) ≤ 1 only when q ≤ √((2τ − 1)p), i.e. q = floor(√((2τ − 1)p)). The B = 50 complementary pairs, the lasso-path top-q rule and τ = 0.6 can stay as they are.
reason: Plug the stated q into the stated bound: q²/((2τ − 1)p) with q = (2τ − 1)p equals (2τ − 1)p. At τ = 0.6 that is 0.2p: an E(V) bound of 10 at p = 50 and 200 at p = 1000, not 1. Only the square-root choice q = √((2τ − 1)p) makes the bound equal 1. The bound itself (MB 2010 Thm 1) also needs exchangeability and a selector no worse than random guessing; Shah & Samworth's assumption-free CPSS results bound a different quantity (low-selection-probability variables).

citations.cite: Meinshausen N, Bühlmann P. Stability selection. JRSS B 2010;72:417-473, Theorem 1: E(V) ≤ q²/((2π_thr − 1)p)
Shah RD, Samworth RJ. Variable selection with error control: another look at stability selection. JRSS B 2013;75:55-80 (arXiv:1105.5578)

bite_note: With p in the tens to thousands, q = 0.2p lets each subsample's lasso choose a fifth of the predictors. The guarantee is gone: the bound allows 0.2p false selections instead of 1, and the selected set fills with noise variables while the app tells the researcher false selections are controlled at about one.

narrowest_regime: A partition (energy-partition) model whose other-source energy is computed as total energy minus kcal-per-unit × exposure, with the addition contrast defined as 'exposure +1 unit, other-source energy unchanged'
reason: In the partition model the covariates are the exposure X and E_other = E_total − c·X, where c is the exposure's kcal per unit. Holding E_other fixed while X rises by 1 requires E_total to rise by c, which is just the identity. If E_total were held fixed instead, E_other would fall by c and the contrast would quietly become an isocaloric substitution of the exposure for other sources, a different estimand (Tomova et al. 2022 distinguish the partition model's addition estimand from the leave-one-out substitution estimand).

citations.cite: Tomova GD, Arnold KF, Gilthorpe MS, Tennant PWG. Adjustment for energy intake in nutritional research: a causal inference perspective. Am J Clin Nutr 2022;115:189-198

bite_note: Building the high setting with total energy fixed would report a substitution effect under an 'addition' label. The two can differ in sign for energy-dense exposures, such as sugar where calories themselves affect the outcome.

failing_part: Absolute risks cannot be predicted from individually matched case-control sets, as a limit of the design
narrowest_regime: When only the matched sample is in hand: no external incidence by matching strata, no sampling fractions, no cohort risk sets
reason: Two parts are right: the conditional likelihood conditions away each set's intercept, and matching makes the sampling fraction vary across matching strata, so no single offset recalibrates. But that limits the sample alone, not the design. Absolute risk is routinely recovered by combining case-control relative risks with external stratum-specific incidence (Gail et al. 1989 used matched BCDDP case-control data this way), and for nested case-control sets drawn from a known cohort, absolute risk is estimable from the sampled risk sets (Borgan et al. 1995; Langholz & Borgan 1997). The cited Janes & Pepe 2008 paper is about ROC/classification accuracy and incremental value under matching, not absolute risk prediction, so it does not support the refusal as phrased.

citations.cite: Janes H, Pepe MS. Matching in studies of classification accuracy: implications for analysis, efficiency, and assessment of incremental value. Biometrics 2008;64:1-9
Borgan O, Goldstein L, Langholz B. Methods for the analysis of sampled cohort data in the Cox proportional hazards model. Ann Stat 1995;23:1749-1778
Langholz B, Borgan O. Estimation of absolute risk from nested case-control data. Biometrics 1997;53:767-774
Gail MH et al. Projecting individualized probabilities of developing breast cancer for white females who are being examined annually. JNCI 1989;81:1879-1886

bite_note: Refusing is the right default when the researcher has only the matched sets. But a researcher whose sets are nested in a known cohort, or who has registry incidence by the matching factors, is told absolute risk is impossible when it is estimable. Saying 'needs external incidence or cohort sampling information' would change their next step.

narrowest_regime: Self-reported energy intake (FFQ or recalls) with an adiposity-related outcome and exclusion of under-reporters by an EI-to-requirement cutoff (e.g. Goldberg)
reason: Recovery-biomarker studies show energy under-reporting is systematic, about 28% on average on FFQs, and that BMI strongly predicts it (Freedman et al. 2014 pooled 5 studies; OPEN). Goldberg-type cutoffs also put predicted BMR, which is a function of body weight, in the denominator. So excluding flagged under-reporters selects on a function of the adiposity outcome, a non-random, outcome-related slice. 'Concentrated' slightly overstates a pervasive bias that grows with BMI, and keeping everyone leaves BMI-differential measurement error rather than removing bias. But the warning as stated is correct and does not claim that keeping everyone is unbiased.

citations.cite: Freedman LS et al. Pooled results from 5 validation studies of dietary self-report instruments using recovery biomarkers for energy and protein intake. Am J Epidemiol 2014;180:172-188
Subar AF et al. Using intake biomarkers to evaluate the extent of dietary misreporting in a large sample of adults: the OPEN study. Am J Epidemiol 2003;158:1-13
Livingstone MBE, Black AE. Markers of the validity of reported energy intake. J Nutr 2003;133 Suppl 3:895S-920S

bite_note: It changes whether a researcher drops flagged under-reporters in a diet-adiposity analysis. Dropping them is selection on the outcome and can create or erase a diet-BMI association, so they would keep everyone and run exclusion as a sensitivity analysis.

failing_part: standard multiple imputation, which assumes it is, is an improvement
narrowest_regime: The first half holds: FFQ blanks often mean never/rarely, older participants omit more items, and that missingness is MNAR. MI under MAR improves only on complete-case estimates of descriptive intake, and only slightly.
reason: Michels & Willett (2009) found 64% of omitted items were later marked never or under once a month, and older women omitted more, so blanks are MNAR. But they concluded that treating blanks as zero is reasonable, not that MI is better. In a simulation (blank in 50-80% of never-users vs 2-5% of users), mean intake was 0.89 true, 0.85-0.88 zero-fill, 1.01-1.12 MI with the outcome (PMM), 1.05-1.20 complete case. For the intake-outcome coefficient (true 0.5), complete case was unbiased (0.50-0.51), as theory predicts when missingness depends on the covariate alone, while MI drifted to 0.51-0.53. So MI is not reliably 'an improvement': zero-fill wins for intake, and complete case is at least as good for the association.

citations.cite: Michels KB, Willett WC. Self-administered semiquantitative food frequency questionnaires: patterns, predictors, and interpretation of omitted items. Epidemiology 2009;20:295-301
White IR, Carlin JB. Bias and efficiency of multiple imputation compared with complete-case analysis for missing covariate values. Stat Med 2010;29:2920-2931

bite_note: The drawer steers researchers from zero-fill toward MI. With blank-means-never data that overstates intake for blank responders and can do worse than complete case for exposure-outcome estimates. A researcher reading it correctly would zero-fill, perhaps with a blank-count indicator or a sensitivity analysis.

failing_part: Multiple imputation with the outcome in the imputation model is invalid under prediction ... under prediction blanks must be filled in each training fold without the outcome
narrowest_regime: Prediction where predictors will also be missing at deployment, and always for the held-out or validation rows, whose own outcomes must never feed their imputations
reason: The leakage half is right: imputing held-out rows from their own outcomes inflates validation performance, and an imputation model that needs Y cannot run on a new row with missing predictors. But the claim's own source, Sisk et al. 2023, concludes that with complete data at deployment the outcome should be used to impute the development data under MI. Only when missingness is allowed at deployment is omitting it preferred. So MI with the outcome in the training-fold imputation is not invalid under prediction in general.

citations.cite: Sisk R, Sperrin M, Peek N, van Smeden M, Martin GP. Imputation and missing indicators for handling missing data in the development and deployment of clinical prediction models: a simulation study. Stat Methods Med Res 2023;32:1461-1477
Moons KGM et al. Using the outcome for imputation of missing predictor values was preferred. J Clin Epidemiol 2006;59:1092-1101

bite_note: When the model will be deployed on complete predictors, refusing outcome-inclusive MI at development forces outcome-free imputation. Under MI that attenuates the coefficients of imputed predictors and degrades calibration, the very thing Sisk et al. recommend against in that regime. A conditional rule (outcome in for training-fold MI when deployment is complete, out otherwise, never for held-out rows) would change the default.

narrowest_regime: Design-based Taylor-linearized estimation in NHANES-style stratified multistage designs, taking 'PSUs minus strata' to count only the PSUs and strata that contain domain rows
reason: NHANES Analytic Guidelines 2011-2016 §3.2.3 say the entire weighted file must be read in, with the subgroup flagged by a SUBPOPN/DOMAIN statement rather than by subsetting. §3.2.3.2 says a subgroup's df should be based on the number of strata and PSUs containing the observations of interest (PSUs minus strata, e.g. 25 − 13 = 12). NCHS uses Taylor series linearization, and the with-replacement treatment of first-stage units (MVUs) is the standard approximation for it. Deleting rows can drop whole PSUs or strata and treats the domain size as fixed, which misstates the SEs. Under the claim's wording, the variance machinery is right; using complete cases as a domain changes the estimand, which the claim does not address.

citations.cite: NCHS. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey: Analytic Guidelines, 2011-2016 (Johnson CL et al.), §3.2.1 (Taylor series linearization), §3.2.3 subsetting data, §3.2.3.2 degrees of freedom
West BT, Berglund P, Heeringa SG. A closer examination of subpopulation analysis of complex-sample survey data. Stata J 2008;8:520-531

bite_note: Subsetting before analysis gives wrong standard errors, and full-design df of 15 instead of the domain's reduced df gives too-narrow t intervals, for subgroups such as a race group represented in only some locations. Domain analysis with reduced df changes the reported CIs and p-values.

failing_part: so each site gets its own intercept and cluster-robust intervals (regime includes households and any outcome)
narrowest_regime: Linear (or conditional-likelihood) outcome models with exposure that varies within groups of moderate size, where the site is a common cause of exposure and outcome
reason: Several parts are right: between-group confounding biases the pooled estimate, naive intervals are too narrow when exposure and residuals cluster, cluster-only SEs leave the point estimate untouched, few clusters need CR2 or wild-bootstrap corrections, and grouped CV is right for predicting to new groups. But per-group intercepts fail in part of the stated regime. With a binary outcome and household-sized groups, unconditional logistic regression with one intercept per group suffers incidental-parameter bias: simulated true β = 1 gave 1.96 for pairs, 1.48 for groups of 4 and 1.17 for groups of 10, the classic 2β limit (Andersen 1970; Abrevaya 1997), so conditional logistic or a within/between random-intercept model is needed. Group intercepts also make a group-level exposure (constant within site) unestimable.

citations.cite: Andersen EB. Asymptotic properties of conditional maximum-likelihood estimators. JRSS B 1970;32:283-301
Abrevaya J. The equivalence of two estimators of the fixed-effects logit model. Econ Lett 1997;55:41-43
Cameron AC, Miller DL. A practitioner's guide to cluster-robust inference. J Hum Resour 2015;50:317-372

bite_note: For household or small-batch groups with a yes/no outcome, the default per-group-intercept logit roughly doubles the log-OR, so the reported effect is badly inflated. The natural alternative, conditional logistic or a random intercept with the group mean of the exposure, gives a different and correct estimate.

failing_part: scoring predicted risk ... at the median follow-up time of the training rows is an appropriate default horizon
narrowest_regime: A pragmatic fallback when no clinical horizon exists, provided 'median follow-up' is the reverse-Kaplan-Meier median and enough rows stay at risk and uncensored there for IPCW Brier and calibration to be stable
reason: The only basis offered is the app's own contract, which is an assertion. Methods guidance ties the horizon for time-to-event calibration and Brier scores to the clinical question, with no reason to default to median follow-up. The claim also does not say how the median is taken: the median of observed times (events plus censorings) is shorter than the reverse-KM median follow-up (Schemper & Smith 1996), which pulls the horizon earlier where few events have occurred. The usual alternatives, an integrated Brier score over a range or several horizons, are not shown to be worse, so 'appropriate' is not established.

citations.cite: Schemper M, Smith TL. A note on quantifying follow-up in studies of failure time. Control Clin Trials 1996;17:343-346
Austin PC, Harrell FE, van Klaveren D. Graphical calibration curves and the integrated calibration index (ICI) for survival models. Stat Med 2020;39:2714-2742

bite_note: Brier scores and calibration slopes change with the horizon, and models can swap ranks between an early and a late horizon. The default horizon therefore changes which model looks best and whether calibration looks acceptable.

failing_part: events are ... (smallest class for several classes)
narrowest_regime: Binary and continuous outcomes: counting k − 1 per k-level categorical, every declared spline or quintile column, and k − 2 nonlinear columns per restricted cubic spline with k knots for every predictor eligible for a data-driven bend, on the development (training) rows
reason: Most of the parameter count matches the sources. Riley et al. and pmsampsize count candidate predictor parameters, not predictors, including categorical dummies and nonlinear terms. A restricted cubic spline with k knots has k − 1 parameters, i.e. k − 2 beyond the linear term, and Harrell's knot rule (k = 3 for n < 30, 4 typically, 5 for n ≥ 100) is real. Counting bends chosen by inner CV is right, because candidates count. The multiclass rule is not Riley's: the multinomial extension (Pate et al. 2023) bases the minimum on the Cox-Snell R² and prevalences of each pairwise one-to-one submodel, not on the smallest class's count. Applying Harrell's rule to the effective rather than the total size is the app's own adaptation, defensible but not sourced.

citations.cite: Riley RD et al. Calculating the sample size required for developing a clinical prediction model. BMJ 2020;368:m441
pmsampsize R package documentation: 'parameters' = number of candidate predictor parameters, may exceed number of predictors
Pate A, Riley RD, Collins GS et al. Minimum sample size for developing a multivariable prediction model using multinomial logistic regression. Stat Methods Med Res 2023;32:555-571
Harrell FE. Regression Modeling Strategies, §2.4 (k knots → k − 1 parameters; k = 3 for n < 30, k = 5 for n ≥ 100)

bite_note: For binary or continuous outcomes the count is right and sets the shelf order properly. For outcomes with several classes, the smallest-class shortcut can put the dataset on the wrong side of the minimum compared with Pate's pairwise criteria, which flips whether regression families are shown first. The effect is modest and limited to multiclass outcomes.
